passages.text: “After the old man said this, I understood from his account that the old man he said had died was your father. I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you. But after learning where he was staying and telling him where I was staying, for accuracy’s sake I asked only this: ‘What was the old man’s name?’ He said, ‘Faustus.’ ‘And his twin sons’ names?’ He answered, ‘Faustinus and Faustinianus.’ ‘And the third son’s?’ He said, ‘Clement.’ ‘And what was the name of their mother?’ He said, ‘Mattidia.’ So, joining in the weeping out of sympathy, I dismissed the crowds and came to you, so that after sharing the salt I might consult you about these things. I did not want to tell you before we partook of salt, lest, overcome by grief, you spend the day of baptism in mourning, when even angels rejoice.” While Peter was saying this, all of us were weeping with our mother. Seeing us weep, he said, “Now let each of you bear what has been said courageously through fear toward God. Your father did not die today, but long ago, as you yourselves said in conjecture.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἔλεγεν τεθνάναι γέροντα, αὐτὸς ἦν (ἐξ ὧν ἔλεγεν) ὁ ὑμέτερος πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the old man he said had died was your father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter here identifies the reportedly deceased subject of the story, not yet explicitly the living speaker himself. The old man’s later identity is not read backward into Peter’s present assertion.
The concrete salt-sharing expression is retained in this meal context rather than made an unspecified conversation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐβουλήθην τὸ καθ’ ὑμᾶς αὐτῷ συναντιβαλεῖν, μέχρις ἂν ὑμῖν προσανάθωμαι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personal dative αὐτῷ identifies the old man as the participant in the contemplated conversation. συναντιβαλεῖν suggests bringing accounts together for comparison or exchanging information; “compare your circumstances in discussion with him” is a more explicit alternative. Peter withholds that exchange with the man, not merely an internal comparison with an account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ συμπαθείας οὖν ἐγὼ σύνδακρυς γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: So, joining in the weeping out of sympathy
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύνδακρυς expresses shared weeping, not merely one person’s tears. The main wording retains Peter’s sympathy and joining in tears without specifying an otherwise unexpressed other participant.

passages.text: When Peter said this, my mother could not bear it and cried aloud, “Alas, husband! Loving us, you yourself died without judgment, while we live, see the light, and partake of food.” When this single lament had thus ended, there was the old man, coming in too. Just as he was about to ask the cause of the cry, he looked at the woman and said, “Alas! What does this mean? Whom do I see?” He approached, looked more closely, was seen in turn, and embraced her. Both were fainting from sudden joy; though they wanted to speak to one another, they were seized with speechlessness from their insatiable joy and could not keep control. But after a little while my mother said, “I have you, Faustus, sweetest to me in every way! How are you alive, when just a little earlier we heard you were dead? But these are our sons: Faustinus, Faustinianus, and Clement.” When she said this, we three fell upon him and covered him with kisses, faintly recalling his appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν ἀκριτὶ αὐτὸς μὲν ἐτελεύτησας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Loving us, you yourself died without judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches ἀκριτί to ἐτελεύτησας, dying, reading the lament as contrasting his death with their continuing life. The adverb may mean without discrimination, decision, or deliberation; “without judgment” does not assert that a tribunal, hearing, or legal proceeding was involved. A material alternative attaches it to ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν: “loving us without discrimination/deliberation, you yourself died.” That reading characterizes the manner of his love rather than his dying. The immediate focus on death in the lament motivates the main attachment, but the proximity to the preceding participle leaves the alternative viable and not uniquely settled.
The verb can denote dying or perishing. Their subsequent speech and embrace support deathlike faintness or loss of consciousness here, not actual death followed by resurrection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμαυρῶς πως τὴν μορφὴν αὐτοῦ ἀνεφέρομεν
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean bringing back or reproducing. Their childhood separation supports recollection of his appearance rather than verbally describing it for an unstated audience.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτω δὲ τῆς μιᾶς ταύτης ὀλολυγῆς παυσαμένης, ἰδοὺ καὶ ὁ γέρων εἰσῄει
lexical_decisions.chosen: When this single lament had thus ended, there was the old man, coming in too
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Thus” represents οὕτω, and “there was” preserves ἰδού’s attention-directing, presentational force rather than flattening the entrance to a plain temporal report. The following καί is retained as “too.” This introduces the sudden appearance without adding a new person or gesture.

source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a period after the elided μετ’. The English construes μετ’ with οὐ πολὺ as “after a little while” despite that intervening punctuation. This is a disclosed printed/editorial feature; the Greek period is not deleted or claimed as an OCR error, and no lacuna or missing word is restored.
